questions.question: How does prototypal inheritance work in JavaScript?
questions.title: Prototypes Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link to another object. Property access walks the chain: own properties first, then each prototype up to Object.prototype → null. Methods live on the prototype (shared, one copy); instance data lives on the object (per-instance). class syntax is sugar over this exact mechanism — methods go on the prototype, constructors run per instance. Object.create(obj) makes a new object whose prototype IS obj; new Ctor() makes an object whose prototype is Ctor.prototype.

Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    O[obj.x lookup] --> OW{own property?}
    OW -->|yes| V[return it]
    OW -->|no| P1[obj's prototype .x?]
    P1 -->|no| P2[... up the chain ...]
    P2 -->|hit| V2[return]
    P2 -->|null reached| U[undefined]
    subgraph memory

```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why JavaScript chose delegation over classes (the design history): prototypes came from Self's delegation model — objects referencing objects, no classes at all. The 1995 rush bolted Java-ish syntax (new, constructor functions) onto delegation to win acceptance; ES6 classes (2015) finished the cosmetic job — but the runtime model NEVER changed: no classes exist at runtime, only objects with prototype links. This is why `class` is syntax, not semantics — the classic proof being that class methods are non-enumerable prototype properties and `typeof class === 'function'`.

The shadowing and assignment subtleties (the edge markers): reading walks the chain, WRITING doesn't — but properties with getters/setters on the prototype DO intercept writes (a setter on the proto runs on assignment instead of creating an own property — the pattern behind reactive libraries). The deletion subtlety: `delete obj.x` removes the OWN property — the prototype's x (if any) becomes visible again (delete on the instance doesn't touch the prototype's property, so the method 'reappears' if you delete an own override).

The modern feature additions (the completeness layer): Object.create(null) makes a dictionary with NO prototype — no inherited hasOwnProperty/toString, a clean namespace map. class extends wires __proto__ on TWO levels (Sub.prototype's proto = Super.prototype for method lookup; Sub's own proto = Super for static inheritance) — the detail that makes static methods inherit correctly. And super is resolved via the HOME object's prototype chain (bound to the method's location, not the caller) — the mechanism that makes super work in extended classes while this still points to the instance.
